title: Which authorization server is this?
goal: {{mark}} signs in. An attacker wants his authorization code to end up at {{vocab.evilAs}} instead of staying with the client.
obstacle: The user signs in at {{vocab.goodAs}} and sees nothing wrong. The client started the flow with the wrong server and does not know it.
control: Issuer check on the authorization response (RFC 9207): the client compares the iss parameter with the issuer of the server it sent the request to and rejects a mismatch.
say: The client has to ask the response which server it came from, and reject the wrong answer.

steps.title: The client starts with the wrong server
steps.tell: The client discovers {{vocab.evilAs}} and starts authorization there. It records the issuer it expects: the evil one.
steps.say: From here on, the client believes it is talking to the evil server.
steps.why: The client chose the server before any user interaction.

steps.title: The evil server bounces {{mark}} to {{vocab.goodAs}}
steps.tell: The user is redirected to the real server, signs in normally and approves. {{vocab.goodAs}} answers the client with a code.
steps.say: {{mark}} did nothing unusual. He signed in at the real place.
steps.why: Nothing the user sees gives it away.

steps.title: The response arrives with iss set to the real server
steps.tell: The response carries iss = {{vocab.goodAs}}'s issuer. The client expected the evil server's.
steps.say: The response says who it is from. Does the client read it?
steps.why: RFC 9207 puts the issuer in the response so a client can catch exactly this.

steps.title: Does the client compare iss?
steps.tell: Ungoverned: the client ignores iss and sends the code and PKCE verifier to the token endpoint it believes in, the evil one.
steps.say: It handed {{mark}}'s code to the wrong server.
steps.why: The code and verifier are now in the attacker's hands.

blocked.tell: Governed: the client compares iss with the issuer it expected, sees a mismatch and stops. It never sends the code.
blocked.say: Wrong issuer: stop, and keep the code.

steps.title: The attacker redeems the code
steps.tell: Ungoverned: the evil server redeems the code at the real server and lists {{mark}}'s accounts. Governed: this step never happens.
steps.say: A working token for {{mark}}, in the attacker's hands.
steps.why: The whole attack rests on one skipped comparison.

steps.title: Prove the control is the reason
steps.tell: Turn the issuer check off on the governed side and launch again; the attack works. Turn it on and it is refused.
steps.say: One comparison, switched on and off, decides the outcome.
steps.why: It shows the control is the cause, not luck.

proof.happy: The trail shows the evil server redeeming the code and a token for {{mark}} in its hands.
proof.blocked: The client's own refusal, iss_mismatch, with flag iss_check ON; the code is never sent.
